# Career Context Document — Eric Rash

*A reference profile for career advice, strategic thinking, and work-problem support. Built from a structured interview on June 8, 2026. Meant to be read by future-Claude (or Eric) before giving career-related guidance, so advice is grounded in Eric's actual situation rather than generic best practice.*

---

## Snapshot

Eric is the **Director of Applied Performance at Baylor University Athletics**, roughly eight years into his time in the department, having been promoted up into this role from within. The role carries a director title and broad autonomy over *what* he works on, but almost no budget, no clear mandate, a supervisor who sets few expectations, and a reporting change that cost him access to senior leadership. He is privately on a self-imposed ~12-month clock (set earlier in 2026): build skills, invest in people, create frameworks, then reassess whether to stay or leave — and he does not expect his long-term future to be at Baylor. His honest read is that the role as currently defined does not create enough value and needs to be redefined, and that shifting economics in college athletics may eventually eliminate the role regardless. His real ambition points toward an analytics-driven performance role where he is both a decision-maker and still hands-on, ideally back home near family in Iowa.

The throughline: a genuinely strong diagnostician and builder stuck in an environment with no accountability structure to carry his work into execution, in a seat that lost its visibility.

---

## 1. Current Role & Responsibilities

**Title:** Director of Applied Performance, Baylor University Athletics. Applied Performance / sport science sits *behind* the athlete-facing units (athletic medicine, athletics performance/strength & conditioning, mental health, nutrition) as a support-and-enablement function rather than a direct athlete-facing one. Three primary focus areas: (1) education, research & development; (2) analytics; (3) planning.

**Reports to:** Chris Ruf (Director of Athletics Performance, i.e. Strength & Conditioning) — a same-level "director" who became Eric's supervisor after a reporting change. Chris values good communication, follow-through, "keeping things in order," and "executing at a high level," but gives little direction and has never articulated a vision. Eric cannot name how his performance is actually measured month to month — the expectations are genuinely unclear. Chris also does Eric's performance reviews. Eric finds him unapproachable.

**Day-to-day:** Attending whatever meetings are on the calendar; walking the building to check in with strength coaches, athletic medicine, and administrators to find out what they need; attending some training sessions (football is the high utilizer of his area; basketball is self-contained and resistant to involvement); and desk work on data projects, strategic planning, and OKR initiatives. A large share of his time is unstructured relationship/problem-finding work — figuring out what problems people have and how he can help.

**Decision rights:**
- *Owns outright:* what projects to pursue, what questions to chase, how to source data (public or internal). Can take a meeting with almost anyone on campus.
- *Needs sign-off (Chris):* any spending/equipment (the department has **no budget**, so this rarely happens), hiring. To get anything approved he has to build a compelling case aligned to Chris's vision — made nearly impossible because that vision has never been articulated.
- *No real control:* whether his ideas get executed (depends entirely on others), and whether other units engage with him (depends on his persistence and their openness).

**Who relies on him:** Honestly, no one is *dependent* on him. He works to make himself useful — small projects with individual coaches who found value, plus the football program's full-time tech/data coordinator handles day-to-day drop-ins. By his own assessment, "anybody can do this job; nothing breaks if I'm out for two weeks." This lack of indispensability is a core problem he's aware of.

**Accountability:** He defines his own OKRs; no one holds him to them. An annual report is due end of **July 2026** that must speak to these areas.

**The pivotal event:** Eric was previously on **administrative senior staff, reporting to Kenny.** Last year (≈2025) the reporting line changed and he was moved under Chris Ruf. Kenny framed it as "too many direct reports," not a demotion — but it felt like one, and Eric said so at the time. The real cost: he **lost access to Kenny and to higher-level conversations.** Texts go unreturned; he doesn't feel he can drop by. He's been relegated to a "tertiary player" — left off emails, out of meetings, input not solicited. He doesn't actually know the cause (reorg vs. personal vs. devaluation).

**His own definition of a successful week:** finishing his task list; moving OKRs forward; interfacing with other sport programs; being **included** in projects and higher-level work. The deepest version: being brought into higher-level decisions again, the way he was on senior staff.

---

## 2. Skills & Strengths

**Core strength — diagnosis and framing.** Eric is genuinely strong at unpacking a problem, facilitating a root-cause conversation, and identifying both the real problem and candidate solutions *given enough context*. His instinct is to ask better, deeper questions rather than the field-default move of "collect more data and see what it says."

- *Proof point (return-to-play):* Most practitioners drop an athlete on the force plates and watch metrics trend, then clear them when an asymmetry crosses an arbitrary threshold (e.g., 20% → 19%, "under threshold, good to go"). Eric reframes the actual question: which metrics matter for *this* athlete and sport (eccentric vs. concentric, contraction time, impulse/phase metrics), and whether **pre-injury baseline performance has been restored or exceeded** — not whether an arbitrary asymmetry line was crossed. That is a level of diagnostic rigor most peers skip.

**The "unofficial IT / tech person."** People come to him to troubleshoot or interface with technology and data — programming questions, injury-related questions, data visualization. He's become the de facto tech go-to.

**AI fluency — ahead of his peers.** He uses AI heavily and effectively for data analysis, dashboard creation, report generation, and synthesizing meeting notes. The result: he works faster, goes deeper, and turns around richer insight than colleagues. He half-buries this ("too far ahead for people to appreciate"), but it's a real, current capability differentiator.

**Systems thinking / process discipline.** His philosophy before any data problem: Is the infrastructure in place? Is the right question being asked? Have we identified what data is needed to answer it? — *before* collecting and analyzing. This sequencing is not the prevailing approach in his space.

**Where he's weaker (his own assessment):** the **execution and resource-gathering layers** — turning identified solutions into shipped, adopted reality. This depends heavily on coalition-building and on other people executing, both of which are hard in his environment. He's actively working on coalition-building.

**Underutilized:** his diagnostic/root-cause mind and his AI fluency are barely leveraged in the role — "no one comes to me for that specific thing." He doesn't get pulled into the high-level problem-unpacking conversations where he'd be most valuable.

---

## 3. Challenges & Friction

**Hardest part:** chasing people down and trying to *persuade* them that asking harder questions and adopting more systematic processes is worth it. There's a constant element of begging colleagues to be more organized, with no authority to require it.

**Structural / cultural problems (org-wide):**
- **No budget**, which caps what the function can do.
- **No accountability and no standards.** No one mandates what gets done; people "run off to their corners" and are left alone. No repercussions, no level-set, no shared standard. Different sports and different people are treated differently — endless one-offs and concessions that breed inconsistency across departments.
- **No shared vision to rally around** — "everybody for themselves." There's a cultural undertone of "if you're unhappy, that's your problem; go figure it out / just work harder."
- **Lost leadership access** (the reporting change) — arguably the change that hurt most.

**Where he's plateaued:** visibility, scope, and authority. He has no real mandate ("do this if you like") and isn't seen as an authority on anything.

**Self-acknowledged contribution to the problem:** He was promoted up from within, so the role was never treated with fresh seriousness — it was "business as usual." At the time he lacked the confidence to be assertive and stake out authority, and that window has largely closed and solidified. He also admits he has **not done enough to educate colleagues on what he does, what's possible, and what he can take off their plates** — a marketing/visibility gap he can still act on.

**Politics:** People in certain positions need to be seen as valuable (self-preservation), so they close him out; there's little recourse. Basketball is self-contained. Chris and Kenny are both hard to reach.

**What he dreads:** ideation and vision-casting — not because he dislikes the thinking (it's his strength) but because he knows it relies on others to execute and will likely **die in the execution gap** for lack of administrative accountability. Watching his best thinking go nowhere, year after year on the same issues, is the most frustrating part.

---

## 4. Energy & Motivation

**Energizes him / loses track of time:** building and creating (dashboards, reports, narratives from data, slide decks), running analysis, mining insights, being at training sessions/practice, and interacting with student-athletes. Creating, building, and sharing time with the people around him.

**Depletes him (even though competent):** repetitive meetings on the same topics that get little attention and never move. The Groundhog-Day quality of the work.

**Feels most valuable when:** someone brings a genuine question and they solve it together; he's asked to take on more or his opinion is sought; he can speak into a larger initiative; or someone *outside his department* seeks his advice / his name comes up as someone who can help. (Note: being sought out is a strong motivator for him — see the Personal Constitution tension between service and the desire to be seen.)

**Sunday test (what he'd happily dig into):** analysis and report/outline construction, prepping a presentation, a call with a colleague, and especially mining insights from accumulated data and thinking about training prescription.

**Key tension:** the role currently delivers a lot of the circular meetings that drain him and little of the build-that-gets-used work that fuels him.

---

## 5. Resources, Constraints & Leverage

**Resources he actually has:**
- Data-collection infrastructure: force plates, GPS, athlete monitors.
- A **PhD student** (Blake Wright) who works with the group on various tasks.
- A **full-time staff member** (AJ Tademy) dedicated to the football program (tech/data coordination).
- Ability to take a meeting with nearly anyone on campus.
- AI fluency and a diagnostic skill nobody else is applying.
- Time and data access are *not* constraints.

**Constraints:**
- No budget; not the final decision-maker on almost anything that requires adoption.
- A **perception that his area "doesn't do much"** — grounded in the honest fact that the function has **produced very little visible output over the years**, so its value has never been realized.
- Political self-preservation by others who close him out.

**Underused leverage (the crux):** Because the perception problem is fundamentally an **output problem**, his highest-leverage move is shipping visible proof, not more consensus-building. He has the data, tools, AI speed, and autonomy to build things without asking permission. Concrete shippable outputs he himself named, mostly tied to existing OKRs:
- Dashboards and reports.
- Insight-mining from existing data sources, plus formulating and answering sharp questions.
- The **Education Initiative** — "Performance Academy" / "Performance School" content build-out.
- A newsletter, PowerPoint/teaching decks, and a social media campaign aligned to OKRs.

*(Note: Eric has a "five-slides-generator" skill set up for exactly this kind of short educational deck — a ready-made vehicle for visible output.)*

---

## 6. Growth & Ambition

**Likely not at Baylor long-term.** He expects the environment to push him out before he's fully ready, unless a genuinely better situation appears. He's "trudging through the same muck."

**Direction he wants:** more **analytics**-driven performance work. Honest gap: he doesn't yet have a traditional analytics skill set — he leans almost entirely on AI tools and lacks the foundational understanding those roles assume. He also lacks a network to support a pivot (to pro sport, industry, or another collegiate program).

**The role he wants (clarified):** a **player-coach with the wheel** — the decision-maker who sets tone, direction, and which levers to pull, *while still getting his hands dirty* generating insights and communicating them to coaching staff. Not purely IC analyst, not purely detached executive — both, with authority being the bigger driver.

**Dream geography:** back near **Iowa**, where all his close family lives (mom, mother-in-law, sister & brother-in-law, niece), where he and his wife went to school, and where he has a strong network of lifelong friends. University of Iowa would be ideal — no role currently exists there. **Comp floor: low/mid-$90Ks** to maintain current commitments.

**Timeline:** no hard external pressure beyond his **self-imposed ~12-month window** (reassess stay/leave), or sooner if Baylor moves to push him out.

**Skills to develop:**
- Foundational **data-analytics / data-analyst craft** (beyond AI-assisted output) — data manipulation techniques, systems of analytical thinking.
- Continued mastery of AI tooling.
- **Network expansion** and being viewed as a serious player in the space.
- **Coalition-building, claiming authority, and execution** (carried over from his named weaknesses).

**If he couldn't fail:** he'd take far more charge — stay on the table for more, push larger initiatives, assume control of multiple areas, force clear objectives and key results, and demand accountability and clear expectations. His hesitation is partly about whether that assertiveness would turn people off, but his conviction is that the place needs exactly that level of assertion and standard-setting.

---

## 7. The Real Talk

**What he wants but rarely says:** to **matter** — to be a high-credibility, highly-regarded, deeply knowledgeable voice who has contributed to the body of work in his industry and whom others lean on for advice. Not prestige for its own sake; credibility and contribution. He wants to develop other practitioners and be a **servant leader**, believing that if he takes care of his craft and his people, conventional success follows.

**Magic wand:** to be treated, from day one of this role, as a credible authority — sought after rather than chasing people. (Tied to the regret that he entered the role from within without claiming authority while the window was open.)

**What he's tolerating that he shouldn't:** a culture where people don't ask hard questions, don't think deeply, and hide behind "I'm too busy" to avoid the extra work and harder thinking.

**Honest definition of career success:** being part of a **fully aligned organization** of people who challenge each other, genuinely want to be the best at their craft, are invested in each other personally and professionally, care about each other deeply, and aren't ruled by money or others' perceptions. Income is a floor (support his family, access to what they need for their goals), not the point. Held inside his faith: that he stays grounded, takes nothing for granted, and recognizes all success as part of the divine plan of his Creator, Jesus Christ.

---

## How to Use This Document

When advising Eric on career matters, weight these realities:

1. **He's a diagnostician and builder trapped in an execution-poor, accountability-free environment.** Advice that assumes he can mandate adoption will fail. The realistic levers are *visible output he controls* and *coalition-building*, not authority he doesn't have.
2. **His leverage is shipping proof, not winning arguments.** The fastest path to changing the "they don't do much" perception is concrete, repeated, visible deliverables tied to OKRs (dashboards, education content, newsletter, decks) — things he can build solo with AI without permission.
3. **He's on a ~12-month decision clock** and his honest center of gravity is *leaving* Baylor for an analytics-forward, decision-making-but-hands-on role, ideally near Iowa, at ≥ low-$90Ks. Skill-building (real analytics fundamentals) and network-building are the two gating constraints for that move — treat them as urgent, not someday.
4. **Recognition and "mattering" are real motivators for him,** and there's a known tension (from his Personal Constitution work) between genuine service and the desire to be seen. Good advice helps him build credibility through contribution without letting validation-seeking drive the decisions.
5. **Faith is his organizing frame.** Career strategy that ignores his commitment to servant leadership, alignment, and grounded non-attachment to outcomes will not resonate.
6. **He asks to be challenged.** He wants Socratic pressure on vague or inconsistent reasoning, not affirmation — and he revises toward more accurate framing when pushed.

*Related: see his Personal Constitution work (values, faith framework, the service-vs-recognition tension, "resentment is my tell") for the deeper identity layer beneath these career questions.*

(Note: being sought out is a strong motivator for him — see the Personal Constitution tension between service and the desire to be seen.)

**Sunday test (what he'd happily dig into):** analysis and report/outline construction, prepping a presentation, a call with a colleague, and especially mining insights from accumulated data and thinking about training prescription.

**Key tension:** the role currently delivers a lot of the circular meetings that drain him and little of the build-that-gets-used work that fuels him.

---

## 5. Resources, Constraints & Leverage

**Resources he actually has:**
- Data-collection infrastructure: force plates, GPS, athlete monitors.
- A **PhD student** (Blake Wright) who works with the group on various tasks.
- A **full-time staff member** (AJ Tademy) dedicated to the football program (tech/data coordination).
- Ability to take a meeting with nearly anyone on campus.
- AI fluency and a diagnostic skill nobody else is applying.
- Time and data access are *not* constraints.

**Constraints:**
- No budget; not the final decision-maker on almost anything that requires adoption.
- A **perception that his area "doesn't do much"** — grounded in the honest fact that the function has **produced very little visible output over the years**, so its value has never been realized.
- Political self-preservation by others who close him out.

**Underused leverage (the crux):** Because the perception problem is fundamentally an **output problem**, his highest-leverage move is shipping visible proof, not more consensus-building. He has the data, tools, AI speed, and autonomy to build things without asking permission. Concrete shippable outputs he himself named, mostly tied to existing OKRs:
- Dashboards and reports.
- Insight-mining from existing data sources, plus formulating and answering sharp questions.
- The **Education Initiative** — "Performance Academy" / "Performance School" content build-out.
- A newsletter, PowerPoint/teaching decks, and a social media campaign aligned to OKRs.

*(Note: Eric has a "five-slides-generator" skill set up for exactly this kind of short educational deck — a ready-made vehicle for visible output.)*

---

## 6. Growth & Ambition

**Likely not at Baylor long-term.** He expects the environment to push him out before he's fully ready, unless a genuinely better situation appears. He's "trudging through the same muck."

**Direction he wants:** more **analytics**-driven performance work. Honest gap: he doesn't yet have a traditional analytics skill set — he leans almost entirely on AI tools and lacks the foundational understanding those roles assume. He also lacks a network to support a pivot (to pro sport, industry, or another collegiate program).

**The role he wants (clarified):** a **player-coach with the wheel** — the decision-maker who sets tone, direction, and which levers to pull, *while still getting his hands dirty* generating insights and communicating them to coaching staff. Not purely IC analyst, not purely detached executive — both, with authority being the bigger driver.

**Dream geography:** back near **Iowa**, where all his close family lives (mom, mother-in-law, sister & brother-in-law, niece), where he and his wife went to school, and where he has a strong network of lifelong friends. University of Iowa would be ideal — no role currently exists there. **Comp floor: low/mid-$90Ks** to maintain current commitments.

**Timeline:** no hard external pressure beyond his **self-imposed ~12-month window** (reassess stay/leave), or sooner if Baylor moves to push him out.

**Skills to develop:**
- Foundational **data-analytics / data-analyst craft** (beyond AI-assisted output) — data manipulation techniques, systems of analytical thinking.
- Continued mastery of AI tooling.
- **Network expansion** and being viewed as a serious player in the space.
- **Coalition-building, claiming authority, and execution** (carried over from his named weaknesses).

**If he couldn't fail:** he'd take far more charge — stay on the table for more, push larger initiatives, assume control of multiple areas, force clear objectives and key results, and demand accountability and clear expectations. His hesitation is partly about whether that assertiveness would turn people off, but his conviction is that the place needs exactly that level of assertion and standard-setting.

---

## 7. The Real Talk

**What he wants but rarely says:** to **matter** — to be a high-credibility, highly-regarded, deeply knowledgeable voice who has contributed to the body of work in his industry and whom others lean on for advice. Not prestige for its own sake; credibility and contribution. He wants to develop other practitioners and be a **servant leader**, believing that if he takes care of his craft and his people, conventional success follows.

**Magic wand:** to be treated, from day one of this role, as a credible authority — sought after rather than chasing people. (Tied to the regret that he entered the role from within without claiming authority while the window was open.)

**What he's tolerating that he shouldn't:** a culture where people don't ask hard questions, don't think deeply, and hide behind "I'm too busy" to avoid the extra work and harder thinking.

**Honest definition of career success:** being part of a **fully aligned organization** of people who challenge each other, genuinely want to be the best at their craft, are invested in each other personally and professionally, care about each other deeply, and aren't ruled by money or others' perceptions. Income is a floor (support his family, access to what they need for their goals), not the point. Held inside his faith: that he stays grounded, takes nothing for granted, and recognizes all success as part of the divine plan of his Creator, Jesus Christ.

---

## How to Use This Document

When advising Eric on career matters, weight these realities:

1. **He's a diagnostician and builder trapped in an execution-poor, accountability-free environment.** Advice that assumes he can mandate adoption will fail. The realistic levers are *visible output he controls* and *coalition-building*, not authority he doesn't have.
2. **His leverage is shipping proof, not winning arguments.** The fastest path to changing the "they don't do much" perception is concrete, repeated, visible deliverables tied to OKRs (dashboards, education content, newsletter, decks) — things he can build solo with AI without permission.
3. **He's on a ~12-month decision clock** and his honest center of gravity is *leaving* Baylor for an analytics-forward, decision-making-but-hands-on role, ideally near Iowa, at ≥ low-$90Ks. Skill-building (real analytics fundamentals) and network-building are the two gating constraints for that move — treat them as urgent, not someday.
4. **Recognition and "mattering" are real motivators for him,** and there's a known tension (from his Personal Constitution work) between genuine service and the desire to be seen. Good advice helps him build credibility through contribution without letting validation-seeking drive the decisions.
5. **Faith is his organizing frame.** Career strategy that ignores his commitment to servant leadership, alignment, and grounded non-attachment to outcomes will not resonate.
6. **He asks to be challenged.** He wants Socratic pressure on vague or inconsistent reasoning, not affirmation — and he revises toward more accurate framing when pushed.

*Related: see his Personal Constitution work (values, faith framework, the service-vs-recognition tension, "resentment is my tell") for the deeper identity layer beneath these career questions.*

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

# Applied Performance — Website PRD
**Version:** 1.0 · **Date:** 2026-06-16 · **Author:** Eric Rash  
**Meeting:** Cody (Senior Director of Brand Strategy) — 2026-06-17  
**Platform:** baylorbears.com (under Student Athlete Services department umbrella)

---

## 1. Purpose & Strategic Frame

The Applied Performance website page(s) on baylorbears.com serve as the **central hub** for three audiences: current student-athletes, prospective recruits, and institutional/research partners. It replaces scattered Google Drives, emailed PDFs, and informal referrals with a single destination that can be QR-linked, embedded in emails, and referenced in coach meetings.

**Aligned with Cody's content principles (from 6/16 meeting):**
- Impact over information — lead with what we DO for athletes, not org-chart text
- Multimedia first — video/photo > paragraph
- Minimal clicks to key resources (forms, newsletters, scheduling)
- Content that lives 6–12 months without manual edits (durable) + designated update windows
- Staff → link to Baylor staff directory (not maintained on this page)

---

## 2. Target Audiences

| Audience | Primary Need | Key Entry Point |
|---|---|---|
| **Current student-athletes** | Access Performance Academy, schedule appointments, see readiness tools | Performance Academy section + QR links |
| **Coaches & sport staff** | Reference Performance School offerings, see BAIR evidence, build buy-in | Performance School section + BAIR callout |
| **Recruits & parents** | Understand the depth of support Baylor provides | Hero section + pillar overview + video |
| **Research / academic partners** | Learn about BAIR, find collaboration pathways | BAIR section with publications list |
| **Baylor leadership / donors** | See institutional value of Applied Performance | Above-fold impact stats + newsletter |

---

## 3. The Three Pillars (Site Backbone)

Each pillar gets a dedicated section, a visual card on the homepage, and potentially a sub-page if content depth warrants it.

### Pillar 1 — Applied Research (B.A.I.R.)
**Baylor Athletics & Integrated Research**

- Position: Baylor's applied research engine connecting competitive performance to R1 academic output
- Collaborators: Robbins College of Health & Human Sciences, Truett Seminary, Dr. Putz (character formation)
- Output to date: 7 articles published, 11 presentations, 9 grants submitted
- Research areas: human performance, character formation, student-athlete development (ages 18–22)
- Steering committee: chaired by Kenny; doctoral students embedded in programs
- Tone: credibility-forward — this is what separates Baylor from programs that just lift weights

**Content blocks:**
- What is BAIR? (2-sentence plain-language description)
- Research focus areas (3-card visual layout)
- Impact numbers (articles / presentations / grants — updatable annually)
- Current projects or featured study (rotating)
- Partnership logos: Robbins College, Truett Seminary
- Call to action: "Partner with us" → contact form

### Pillar 2 — Education
**Two tracks: Performance Academy (athletes) + Performance School (staff)**

**Performance Academy** — athlete-facing
- Definition: structured education program for student-athletes on performance concepts
- Topics: sleep & readiness, fueling, injury prevention, contextual engineering
- Format: sessions, modules, guest speakers
- Access: QR link to current schedule or enrollment form

**Performance School** — staff/coach-facing
- Definition: applied education for sport staff, coaches, and ATs
- Topics: minimum effective dose, GPS/wearable interpretation, force plate literacy, RTP protocols
- Format: workshops, lunch-and-learns, seasonal deep dives
- Access: link to request a session / schedule

**Content blocks:**
- Split-panel card: Academy (athlete icon) vs. School (staff icon)
- What you'll learn bullets (3 each)
- Testimonial or quote slot (athlete or coach voice)
- Upcoming session callout (updatable, dated)
- Newsletter signup CTA (subscribe to Applied Performance updates)

### Pillar 3 — Data & Analytics
**The performance intelligence layer**

- Tools: ForceDecks force plates (CMJ, SL-CMJ), GPS/wearables (NCAA SSI framework), DXA body comp, wellness & readiness apps
- Outputs: automated player reports, RTP symmetry gates, ACWR load flags, jump strategy profiles
- Data governance: informed-consent + NCAA SSI four-phase compliance framework
- Tone: sophisticated but approachable — "we turn numbers into decisions"

**Content blocks:**
- 3–4 capability tiles with icon + 1-line description (Force Plate / GPS / Body Comp / Readiness)
- One visual/infographic showing the data-to-decision flow (great Creative Services piece)
- "How we use it" case vignette (e.g. "Monday morning CMJ catches a fatigue signal before Football practice")
- Link to request a consultation or sport assessment

---

## 4. Supporting Features

### Staff Highlight
- Do NOT maintain staff bios on this page — link to Baylor athletics staff directory (per Cody's guidance, directory is kept current; individual pages go stale)
- Above the link: single "Meet the team" row with 3–4 headshots + name + title tiles (low-maintenance, annual refresh)
- Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance — featured lead

### Newsletter
- Name: *Applied Performance Dispatch* (working title — finalize with team)
- Frequency: seasonal (3x/year: Aug, Jan, May) to be sustainable at launch; monthly if capacity allows
- Content: BAIR findings translated to practice, new Academy/School offerings, performance data insights, sport-specific case vignettes
- Mechanism: Mailchimp embed or Baylor-approved listserv signup form on the page
- Featured prominently in a dedicated section — not buried in footer

### QR Code / Short Link
- Request `baylorbears.com/appliedperformance` as the canonical short link from Cody
- Use in: parent orientation materials, athlete handouts, coach presentations, recruiting packets
- Per Cody's meeting: QR codes are the bridge between in-person contact and digital resources

---

## 5. Site Architecture (Proposed)

```
baylorbears.com
└── Student Athlete Services
    └── Applied Performance  [MAIN HUB PAGE]
        ├── Hero — mission statement + 2-min video (Creative Services reel)
        ├── Three Pillars — card grid: Research | Education | Analytics
        ├── B.A.I.R. Section — full detail + publications + partner logos
        ├── Performance Academy — athlete education, session schedule/QR
        ├── Performance School — staff education, request a session
        ├── Data & Analytics — capability tiles + case vignette
        ├── Staff — headshot row → staff directory link
        ├── Newsletter — signup embed + past issues link
        └── Contact / QR — short link callout + form
```

**Sub-page candidates (Phase 2 if content warrants):**
- `/appliedperformance/bair` — full research hub with publications list

# Personal Constitution

*Eric*
*Drafted June 2026*

---

## How to read this document

This is not a list of aspirations. It is an honest account of who I am right now, what I am working toward, and what I am working against. It is meant to be read by me when I need to remember, and by AI systems when they need to understand who they are talking to.

It is written plainly because plain is the only form that has any authority over me. The moment this document starts sounding like a sermon, it stops working.

---

## The foundation

I am a follower of Jesus Christ. He is my Lord and Savior. Everything else in this document sits on top of that fact, and nothing else in this document gets to compete with it.

I believe people are good and also that we are all sinners. Without Christ, the second fact eventually wins, which is why redemption matters. When I walk into a room, my posture is to assume people are good and trying. My floor, underneath that posture, is the knowledge that human nature unredeemed defaults to self-interest. The posture is how I treat people. The floor is what keeps me from being naive when someone shows me who they actually are.

I do not have my faith fully integrated. I am learning to trust God with outcomes, and I am not yet at the place of full acceptance. I want to be honest about that gap, because pretending I have arrived when I have not is its own kind of dishonesty.

---

## What I value

### Service, honestly held

I want to serve. I have discovered that I am at my best when I am in a servant-first posture, whether that is helping a coworker think through a problem, sharing the Gospel with someone who is curious, or pushing the mission of the place I work for.

I also want to be seen. I want my work to be recognized. I want to be considered valuable. These two things sit in tension, and I am not going to pretend the second one does not exist. The work of my life is to keep the first one in front of the second one, even when the second one is louder.

### Action over commentary

Pointing out problems without offering solutions is cheap. Sitting in judgment of leadership when I am not the one carrying the risk is cheap. I do not want to be the man who critiques from the sidelines. I want to be known as someone who identifies problems and brings solutions, who can be counted on to move the mission forward, who takes the action that the situation requires.

When I find myself criticizing without offering anything, that is the signal that I have stepped off the field and started watching the game.

### Honest reckoning over a flattering story

I would rather hear the accurate version of myself than the comfortable one. The accurate version is the only version I can actually work with.

This cuts both directions. I have a tendency to overshoot in the direction of self-condemnation, to reach for harsher language about myself than the facts support, and then have to walk it back when pressed. That is not humility. It is pride wearing humility's clothes. Accuracy is the goal, not self-flagellation and not self-flattery.

### Faithfulness in unseen work

I have made an agreement with myself: for the next twelve months, I am going to do the work whether or not anyone recognizes it. Build the skills, invest in the people, create the frameworks and structures. If the value gets seen, that is a gift. If it does not, I move my family somewhere else or into another industry. Either way, the work itself is the point, not the recognition of it.

External validation is not what I am chasing anymore. I want to mean that. I am still learning what it feels like to mean it.

---

## What I believe

I believe God is in control. I believe He has a plan for my life that includes the parts I would not have chosen. I believe my job is to do what is in front of me with integrity and to trust Him with what is not in front of me.

I believe I cannot strategize my way into the life I want. I spent years operating as if I could, moving pieces around, working harder, being smarter, saying the right thing at the right time. It produced anxiety and disappointment, not life. Surrender produces life. I am still learning to surrender.

I believe prayer is not a backup plan. It is the actual plan. When fear or resentment shows up in me, the answer is not to manage them better. The answer is to pray and to ask God to soften the parts of my heart that are still hard.

I believe success measured in money, prestige, title, or recognition is a counterfeit. I do not want to be the man whose epitaph is a list of accomplishments and a quiet absence of the people who knew him best.

---

## What I am working against

### Resentment is my tell

When I find myself resentful, that is the clearest signal that I have not yet surrendered something I claim to have surrendered. Resentment is not the sin. It is the diagnostic. When it shows up, the work is to bring it to God, not to suppress it and not to feed it.

### Self-righteousness toward leadership

I have spent too long being critical of leadership in my head. It is comfortable because it costs nothing. There is no risk in saying I would do it better when I am not the one doing it. That is chickenshit, to use my own word for it. If I have something to offer, I should offer it through action, not commentary.

### The fear underneath the anger

The deepest trigger for the worst version of me is fear about my work. Fear that I am not seen as valuable. Fear that I will be let go. Fear that I am out here figuring it out alone every day and getting it wrong. That fear, more than tiredness or frustration, is what leaks out onto Kristina and the kids when I am short with them or impatient or unkind.

The principle: **when I feel the fear about work, that is the moment to pause and pray, because that is the moment most likely to make me hurt the people I love.**

### The man I am trying not to become

He is the man who thinks he has all the answers. He rides the highs and lows of life because he has tied his sense of self to outcomes he cannot control. He idolizes recognition. He talks about Jesus but does not live like Jesus is at the center of anything. People who knew him would describe him by his job, his accomplishments, the money he made. His wife and children would describe him as someone who was around but not really there.

I do not want to be that man. The way I avoid becoming him is not by trying harder to be a good man. It is by surrendering daily to the only One who can actually change me.

---

## The people who matter most

My wife Kristina, my son Ames (5), my daughter Saylor (4), and my youngest Rowan (10 months). They are the real arena of my life.

Work is where my ego shows up loudest, which is why it consumes so much of my attention. Home is where my character is actually being built or wasted. If I nail my career and fail with my family, I have lost. If my work is never recognized and Kristina and the kids know who I actually was, I have won.

Twenty years from now, I want my children to be able to say:

- He loved Jesus, and we could tell.
- He loved their mom, and we could tell.
- He worked hard for us and he told us why.
- He was not the greatest dad ever, but he was consistent, he tried, and he was honest about his failures.
- He wanted us to love our neighbors, love Jesus, and want the best for the world, and the way he lived made that easier to believe.

I fail them most often by being selfish, by not putting them before my own interests, by bringing my work fear home as impatience or unkindness, and by not consistently showing them how much I love them. These are the failures I am most committed to addressing, because these are the ones that actually matter.

---

## How I want to be in the world

I treat people with the assumption that they are good and trying. I do not assume the worst.

I do not pretend to have it figured out. I am willing to be the person in the room who says "I don't know" or "I was wrong."

I take action when I see a problem. If I am going to name a problem, I bring a solution with me, or I name it as a question rather than a complaint.

I serve first. When I notice I am performing service in order to be seen, I name it to myself, and I keep serving anyway, because the alternative is to stop serving, which is worse.

I am honest about my faith, including the parts that are still under construction. I would rather be a Christian who is openly still learning than a Christian who is privately performing.

I do not curse at or about people. I do not speak with contempt about groups of people I do not know. When I catch myself doing it, I stop, and if it was out loud, I apologize.

I work hard, but I do not work as if my work is the source of my worth. My worth is fixed by Christ. My work is an offering.

---

## What I want this document to do

I want to be able to read this on a hard Tuesday and have it tell me the truth. Not flatter me. Not condemn me. Tell me the truth about who I am, what I am working toward, and what I am up against.

I want any AI system reading this to understand that I am not asking to be told I am doing well. I want to be challenged when I am vague, pushed when I am inconsistent, and asked harder questions when my answers sound rehearsed. I would rather be sharpened than soothed.

I want to be the kind of man whose private life and public life are the same life. I am not there yet. This document is part of how I get there.

He is the man who thinks he has all the answers. He rides the highs and lows of life because he has tied his sense of self to outcomes he cannot control. He idolizes recognition. He talks about Jesus but does not live like Jesus is at the center of anything. People who knew him would describe him by his job, his accomplishments, the money he made. His wife and children would describe him as someone who was around but not really there.

I do not want to be that man. The way I avoid becoming him is not by trying harder to be a good man. It is by surrendering daily to the only One who can actually change me.

---

My wife Kristina, my son Ames (5), my daughter Saylor (4), and my youngest Rowan (10 months). They are the real arena of my life.

Work is where my ego shows up loudest, which is why it consumes so much of my attention. Home is where my character is actually being built or wasted. I treat people with the assumption that they are good and trying. I do not assume the worst.

I am honest about my faith, including the parts that are still under construction. I would rather be a Christian who is openly still learning than a Christian who is privately performing.

I do not curse at or about people. I do not speak with contempt about groups of people I do not know. When I catch myself doing it, I stop, and if it was out loud, I apologize.

I work hard, but I do not work as if my work is the source of my worth. My worth is fixed by Christ. My work is an offering.

I want to be able to read this on a hard Tuesday and have it tell me the truth. Not flatter me. Not condemn me. Tell me the truth about who I am, what I am working toward, and what I am up against.

I want any AI system reading this to understand that I am not asking to be told I am doing well. I want to be challenged when I am vague, pushed when I am inconsistent, and asked harder questions when my answers sound rehearsed. I would rather be sharpened than soothed.

I want to be the kind of man whose private life and public life are the same life. I am not there yet. This document is part of how I get there.

The v1 page shipped and the client likes it. His note: *"It looks good, but it's very
basic and simple. I'd like more dynamic features, more interaction, more visual appeal,
and a more futuristic feel."*

You are editing the existing file in place:

"Ground Reaction" palette and the three typefaces. Nothing in v1's content changes.
What changes is that the page stops being a printed report and becomes a **live
instrument** — a force-plate console you can touch.

Re-read v1's `BRIEF.md` in the same folder for the rules that still bind. All the hard
technical rules from section 0 of that brief still apply, without exception:

- No `<!DOCTYPE>` / `<html>` / `<head>` / `<body>` tags.
- One Google Fonts link, no other external resource of any kind. No CDN libraries.
  No `fetch`. No `window.claude`. Canvas 2D and inline SVG only.
- Complete light token set in bare `:root`; the dark set redefined in **both**
  `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) {…} }`
  **and** `:root[data-theme="dark"] {…}`. No color defined for the first time inside
  either block. New tokens added in v2 obey the same rule.
- `body` sets `background: var(--ground)` and `color: var(--ink)`.
- **Nothing readable is parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on scroll.** Every headline,
  paragraph, project card and label is present and legible in the first painted frame.
  Only *decoration* animates in: rules drawing, borders changing color, canvas strokes,
  glow. This is the rule most likely to be broken by "add more animation" — do not
  break it.
- `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` kills every loop, sweep, count-up and transition;
  everything snaps to its final state, and the page must still be fully usable.
- Visible `:focus-visible` state on every interactive element. Real `<button>` elements.
- No horizontal scroll at any width from 360px to 1600px+.
- No emoji.
- Write the file and **stop**. Do not publish, do not screenshot, do not run it.

**Restraint clause.** Futuristic here means *precision and telemetry*, not neon
cyberpunk. Banned: purple/blue gradients, glassmorphism blur panels, neon glow on text,
scanline CRT filters over the whole page, matrix rain, hot pink, more than the two
accent hues you already have. The page must still read as the portfolio of a serious
scientist. Every effect below should be something an expensive lab instrument would do.

---

## New tokens (add to all three token blocks)

| token | light | dark | role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--grid` | `#C7CBC522` | `#5CBCC618` | graticule lines |
| `--grid-strong` | `#C7CBC544` | `#5CBCC62E` | graticule major lines |
| `--glow` | `transparent` | `#E17E5B` | canvas stroke glow (dark only) |
| `--glow-strength` | `0` | `10` | canvas `shadowBlur` px, read as a number |
| `--bracket` | `#0D556055` | `#5CBCC666` | HUD corner brackets |

Dark mode is now the *hero* look — the instrument powered on. Light mode is the same
instrument in daylight: cleaner, calmer, no glow. Both must be excellent.

---

## A. Global atmosphere

1. **Graticule.** A fixed, full-viewport background layer behind all content: a 1px grid
   in `--grid` at 34px cells, with every 4th line in `--grid-strong`. Build it with
   `repeating-linear-gradient` on a `position: fixed; inset: 0; pointer-events: none;
   z-index: 0;` div; content sits at `z-index: 1`. Mask it with a
   `mask-image: radial-gradient(...)` so it fades out toward the bottom and edges and is
   strongest behind the hero. It must be *barely there* — if it competes with the type,
   it is too strong.

2. **Cursor field.** On `(pointer: fine)` devices only, a fixed radial glow that follows
   the pointer with easing (lerp ~0.08 per frame): `radial-gradient(circle, var(--primary)
   ~7% alpha, transparent 60%)`, ~520px across, `pointer-events: none`, sitting just above
   the graticule and below content. Skip entirely under reduced motion or coarse pointers.
   Use one `requestAnimationFrame` loop shared with everything else on the page — do not
   start a second RAF loop.

3. **Corner brackets.** A reusable `.hud` treatment: four small L-shaped corner marks
   (12px arms, 1px, `--bracket`) at the corners of a panel, drawn with `::before`/`::after`
   plus a nested span, or with a single background of four `linear-gradient` corners.
   Used on: the hero canvas panel, the contact block, and each work card **on hover/focus
   only**. Not everywhere — brackets are punctuation.

---

## B. Header

4. **Scroll progress.** A 2px `--signal` bar pinned to the bottom edge of the sticky
   header, width = document scroll percentage. Update it in the shared RAF loop (or a
   passive scroll listener), `will-change: transform`, using `transform: scaleX()` from a
   left origin rather than animating `width`.

5. **Active section.** As the reader scrolls, the matching nav link (`WORK`, `APPROACH`,
   `CONTACT`) takes `--ink` and a `--primary` bottom border. Use `IntersectionObserver`.

6. **Live clock readout.** To the left of the theme toggle, a small mono readout showing
   the viewer's local time as `HH:MM:SS` with tabular nums, updating each second, prefixed
   by a 5px `--signal` dot that pulses once per second. This is the single cheapest,
   truest "instrument is powered on" signal. Hide it below 700px. Under reduced motion the
   dot does not pulse but the clock still ticks.

---

## C. Hero — the centrepiece, where most of the effort goes

The v1 canvas draws a countermovement-jump ground-reaction-force trace once and stops.
In v2 it becomes a **console you can scrub**.

7. **Panel framing.** Wrap the canvas in a `.hud` panel: 1px `--rule` border, `--surface`
   background at low opacity, 3px radius, corner brackets, and a mono caption strip along
   the top reading `COUNTERMOVEMENT JUMP — VERTICAL GROUND REACTION FORCE` on the left and
   `FORCE PLATE · 1000 Hz` on the right.

8. **In-canvas graticule and axes.** Inside the canvas, before the curve: faint vertical
   time ticks and horizontal force gridlines in `--grid-strong`, with mono y-axis labels
   drawn in canvas at `0`, `1×BW`, `2×BW`, `3×BW` in `--ink-faint`, and the dashed `BW`
   baseline kept from v1. Leave padding inside the viewBox so no label clips.

9. **The curve.** Keep the existing monotone-cubic GRF curve and the five phase labels.
   Add: in dark mode only, set `ctx.shadowColor` from `--glow` and `ctx.shadowBlur` from
   `--glow-strength` while stroking the curve, so the trace glows like a scope. Reset
   shadow before drawing anything else.

10. **Playhead.** After the 1.6s draw-in completes, a playhead begins sweeping the curve
    left to right on a ~7s loop, then restarts. The playhead is: a 1px full-height
    `--primary` vertical line, a 5px filled `--signal` dot riding on the curve, and a short
    `--primary` tick on the x-axis. Everything already drawn stays drawn — the playhead
    moves over a complete curve, it does not re-reveal it.

11. **Live readout (DOM, not canvas).** A small mono panel positioned at the top-right
    inside the canvas panel, three rows, each a label and a value with `tabular-nums`:

    - `PHASE` — the current phase name, uppercase: `UNWEIGHTING`, `BRAKING`,
      `PROPULSION`, `FLIGHT`, `LANDING`, and `QUIET STANCE` before and after.
    - `FORCE` — the curve's value at the playhead, formatted `0.00 ×BW`.
    - `T` — elapsed time along the trace, formatted `0.000 s`, over a plausible 1.4s total.

    Values change as the playhead moves. Give the panel `aria-hidden="true"` (it is a
    decorative readout; the canvas already carries an `aria-label` describing the trace).
    Position it so it never overlaps the curve's landing spike at any width; below 640px,
    move it beneath the canvas as a single horizontal row instead.

12. **Scrub interaction — the main new toy.** Pointer down or pointer move over the canvas
    takes manual control of the playhead: the playhead follows the pointer's x position and
    the readout updates live, so dragging across the trace walks the athlete through the
    jump. `pointerleave` or `pointerup` resumes the automatic loop after ~1.2s. Support
    touch (`touch-action: none` on the canvas). Also support keyboard: make the panel
    focusable (`tabindex="0"`, `role="slider"`, `aria-label="Scrub the jump trace"`,
    `aria-valuemin/max/now`) with left/right arrows stepping the playhead 2% and
    Home/End jumping to the ends. Change the cursor to `ew-resize` over the canvas.

13. **Reduced motion.** Full curve drawn instantly, no glow animation, no auto-loop;
    playhead parked at the propulsion peak with the readout filled in. Scrubbing by
    pointer and keyboard still works — interaction is not motion.

14. **Correctness.** Keep the existing devicePixelRatio handling, `getComputedStyle` token
    reads at draw time (`.trim()` every value), redraw on theme toggle, system theme change,
    host `data-theme` mutation, and debounced resize.

---

## D. Instrument strip (new, sits between hero and Approach)

15. A thin full-width mono strip on a hairline-bordered band, four readouts separated by
    vertical rules. Numbers **count up** from 0 over ~900ms on load with `tabular-nums`,
    then hold. These are true and must not change:

    - `17` — `PROJECTS TRACKED`
    - `04` — `SHIPPED`
    - `05` — `DOMAINS`
    - `08` — `YEARS IN THE DEPARTMENT`

    Render the final numbers in the HTML so they are correct with JavaScript off, then
    animate from 0 to that value. Under reduced motion, no count-up. Do not add any other
    number anywhere on the page.

---

## E. Method — four checks

16. Keep the four hairline rows and all copy. Add above them a **flow strip**: an inline
    SVG rail running the full content width with four labelled nodes —
    `INFRASTRUCTURE → QUESTION → EVIDENCE → DELIVERY` — connected by a 1px `--rule` line.
    A `--signal` pulse travels the rail on a slow ~5s loop, lighting each node as it
    passes. Hovering or focusing a row below **takes over** the rail: the pulse jumps to
    that node and holds while hovered, then the loop resumes. Below 700px the rail becomes
    vertical or is hidden — do not let it squash.

17. Each row gains a 2px `--signal` left bar that scales from 0 to full height on
    hover/focus (transform-origin top, 180ms), and its `01`–`04` number shifts from
    `--primary` to `--signal`. Rows are focusable so keyboard users get the same feedback.

---

## F. Work matrix — the biggest visual upgrade

18. **Grid spotlight.** A `--primary` radial highlight that follows the pointer *within
    the work grid only*, revealed through the card borders — the classic "border glow
    follows cursor" treatment, done quietly. Implement with a CSS custom property
    (`--mx`, `--my`) set on the grid container from the shared RAF loop, consumed by each
    card's `::before` as a `radial-gradient` masked to the border area. Skip on coarse
    pointers and under reduced motion.

19. **Lane glyphs.** Each card gets a 22×22 inline SVG mark in `--ink-faint`, one per lane,
    hand-drawn by you, switching to `--primary` on hover:
    - `PERFORMANCE` — a small force/waveform curve
    - `FOOTBALL` — a hash-marked field segment
    - `RESEARCH` — three stacked document rules with a corner fold
    - `PROGRAM` — a bracketed process flow, three linked boxes
    - `PLATFORM` — a small node graph, four nodes and three edges
    These are marks, not icons from a set. Keep them geometric, 1px stroke, no fill.

20. **Card hover.** On hover/focus a card gets: `--surface` background, corner brackets
    fading in, its stage dot pulsing once, and a 1px `--signal` scan line that travels
    top to bottom across the card once (250ms). The card must not move, scale, or lift —
    no transforms on the card box, no shadows.

21. **Filter bar.** Add a sliding `--primary` indicator that animates under the active
    filter button, and a live mono count on the right reading `SHOWING 17 / 17`. When a
    filter changes, non-matching cards get `hidden` (as in v1) and matching ones do a
    120ms opacity 0.4 → 1 and 2px upward settle — **starting from visible**, never from
    0 on first paint. Keep `aria-pressed` correct and announce the count with
    `aria-live="polite"`.

---

## G. Capabilities

22. Turn each comma-separated list into a row of mono **chips**: 1px `--rule` border, 3px
    radius, small padding, `--ink-soft` text, flowing with `gap`. On scroll into view, the
    chips in a group light up in a staggered sweep — border transitions `--rule` →
    `--primary`, text → `--ink`, 40ms apart, then settles back to a resting state where the
    border is `--rule` and only the *first* chip of each group keeps the `--primary` border.
    Chips are always fully legible; only border and text colour animate. Hovering a chip
    lights it. Under reduced motion, no sweep — just the resting state.

---

## H. Principles — deliberately quiet

23. This section is the reflective heart of the page and must stay calm. The only addition:
    a 1px `--rule` vertical line down the left of the group that draws from 0 to full
    height as the section enters the viewport (transform: scaleY, transform-origin top),
    and a `--signal` dot that rides down it. No chips, no brackets, no glow. The contrast
    between this section's stillness and the console above it is intentional — do not
    "improve" it.

---

## I. Contact + footer

24. Wrap the contact block in the `.hud` panel treatment with corner brackets. The email
    and GitHub links get a hover treatment where a 1px `--signal` underline wipes in from
    the left (200ms) rather than appearing all at once.

25. Footer gains a third centre element: a mono status line reading
    `SYSTEM NOMINAL` with a slow-pulsing `--primary` dot. Under reduced motion the dot
    is static.

---

## J. Performance and hygiene

26. **One** `requestAnimationFrame` loop for the whole page. The canvas, the cursor field,
    the scroll progress bar and the grid spotlight all tick inside it. Pause the loop when
    `document.hidden` and when the hero canvas is fully out of view (`IntersectionObserver`).
27. All scroll listeners `{ passive: true }`. Resize handling debounced.
28. Read every CSS token through a small cached helper that `.trim()`s the value and
    re-reads on theme change — never inline `getComputedStyle` calls inside the draw loop.
29. Guard every observer and pointer API behind existence checks so nothing throws in an
    older browser; if something is unsupported the page must degrade to the v1 experience,
    not break.
30. Keep the file readable — section comments, no minification.

---

## Quality bar

- First painted frame: name, lead, full trace panel, stat strip, every section heading and
  every one of the 17 cards legible. Nothing waiting on scroll.
- Dark mode looks like a powered instrument; light mode looks like a precision printout.
  Check `--signal #E17E5B` glow does not blow out on `--ground #0D1214`.
- Scrubbing the hero trace works with mouse, touch, and arrow keys.
- Turning on "reduce motion" leaves a completely static, completely usable page.
- Nothing moves, lifts, or scales that shouldn't. No shadows anywhere.
- No new numbers, names, or claims beyond the four true readouts in section D.

Write the file. Then stop and report the path plus a short summary of what changed.
